claims.text: High-throughput computational thermodynamic modeling combined with machine learning can accurately determine melting temperatures across a calibrated high-entropy-alloy compositional range.
The combined approach can accurately determine enthalpies and entropies of fusion across that compositional range.
The combined approach can accurately determine volume changes at melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The combined approach is efficient for evaluating large high-entropy-alloy compositional spaces.
The target high-entropy alloys have diverse compositions and near-random multi-principal-element distributions.
Atomic-scale interactions and local chemical environments govern thermodynamic behavior across the solid-liquid transition.
Computational models can capture the fundamental physical interactions and free-energy landscapes relevant to melting.
Machine learning can use existing data to interpolate thermodynamic properties efficiently.
Machine learning can extrapolate thermodynamic properties efficiently.
Predictions of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase properties will be within approximately 5–10% of experimental measurements.
Traditional experimental techniques are generally more time-consuming than the proposed combined approach when exploring large compositional spaces.
Standalone computational methods are generally less precise than the proposed combined approach for exploring large compositional spaces.
Reliable performance is limited to high-entropy alloys within the model's calibrated compositional range.
Reliable performance requires the alloys to maintain single-phase stability under the test conditions.
Accuracy may deteriorate for alloys outside the validated compositional space.
Significant phase segregation or high-temperature non-equilibrium effects may reduce model accuracy.
Differential scanning calorimetry or dilatometry can provide experimental melting temperatures for validation.
Integrated differential-scanning-calorimetry signals can provide fusion enthalpy and entropy for validation.
Dilatometry can provide volume change at melting for validation.
In situ X-ray diffraction can provide the liquid-phase thermodynamic properties needed for validation.

contradictions.description: The rule equates a majority of tested alloys with more than 20% of tested alloys. A majority ordinarily means more than 50%, so the required failure fraction is internally inconsistent.
